question: What is a dressing actually doing, and why is pressure damage a time-and-pressure problem rather than a cleanliness problem?
answer_serious:
# A dressing does not heal anything. It holds a condition in which healing can happen.

This is the single most useful sentence in wound care, and it reframes every product question that
follows from it. Repair is done by the wound: by migrating keratinocytes, by fibroblasts laying
down matrix, by angiogenesis, by the inflammatory cells that clear debris first. A dressing
contributes none of that. **It maintains an environment**, and the environment it maintains is the
thing being chosen when a dressing is chosen. *This is mechanism rather than guideline, and it is
consensus across all major wound-care guidance.*

What the environment consists of:

```
   what a dressing does                     why it matters to the wound itself
   ───────────────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
   holds moisture in the useful range       cells migrate across a moist surface; they
                                            cannot migrate across a dry crust
   manages exudate                          too much floods the peri-wound skin; too
                                            little dries the bed
   keeps temperature stable                 cellular activity falls when the wound is
                                            cooled, and every change cools it
   protects from mechanical trauma           new epithelium is one cell layer thick and
                                            is removed by a wipe
   acts as a bacterial barrier               not sterility — a barrier
   carries information                       wear time, strike-through, what the removed
                                            dressing shows
   does no harm coming off                   an adherent dressing removes what grew
                                            under it; this is a real cost of a change
```

*Which product does which of these is local.* Formularies differ by country and by institution,
and product selection is a decision for the local formulary and the assessing clinician — the
class-level reasoning below is the part that generalises.

## Moisture balance, and why the target is the middle

The historical shift in wound care was from drying wounds out to keeping them moist, and the
mechanism is the whole argument: epithelial cells migrate across a moist surface and have to
tunnel beneath a dry scab. But the opposite extreme is also damage — excess exudate macerates the
peri-wound skin, the barrier fails, and the wound gets *bigger*. So the target is not "wet" and it
is not "dry":

```
   TOO DRY                            right                             TOO WET
   ────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────
   crust forms             │  surface moist, peri-wound   │  peri-wound skin white,
   epithelium has to       │  skin intact, exudate        │  soggy, breaking down
   burrow                  │  contained                   │  wound margin extending
   healing slows           │                              │  dressing leaking
   pain on movement        │                              │  odour, change needed often
   ────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────
   the dressing's job:     DONATE moisture  ◄────────────►  ABSORB moisture

   which is why the classes exist at all, and why they are not interchangeable:
     gels and hydrogels   donate to a dry bed
     foams and alginates  absorb from a wet one
     films                retain, and add nothing
     hydrocolloids        do some of both, within limits
```

The teaching framework for the assessment that precedes the choice is usually some version of
TIME — tissue, infection or inflammation, moisture, and the wound edge. *That framework is widely
taught internationally; it is a teaching structure rather than a regulation.* Its value is the
same as any structured assessment: it stops the moisture question being answered before the tissue
question has been asked.

## Pressure damage is load multiplied by time

Pressure damage is an **ischaemic injury**. Sustained mechanical load deforms soft tissue and
occludes capillary perfusion and lymphatic drainage; oxygen delivery falls, metabolic waste
accumulates, cells are damaged both by the ischaemia and by the deformation itself, and
reperfusion when the load comes off causes further injury. *That mechanism is consensus across
major guidance.*

The relationship that gives the whole topic its shape:

```
   pressure
     ^
   high │ ■
        │   ■
        │      ■
        │          ■ ■
        │                 ■  ■  ■                  everything on or above the
    low │                          ■  ■  ■  ■  ■   curve causes damage
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────►  time
          minutes                                    hours

   HIGH pressure for a SHORT time, or LOW pressure for a LONG time, do the same thing.
   This is why "he was only in the chair for the afternoon" is not reassurance, and why
   a hard edge for twenty minutes is not either.

   Three things move the curve DOWN — i.e. make damage happen sooner:
     SHEAR      tissue layers slide over each other; vessels are stretched and kinked
                as well as compressed. Sliding down the bed is the classic source
     FRICTION   surface damage from rubbing, which also removes the barrier
     MICROCLIMATE  moist, warm skin at the interface tolerates less load than dry,
                cool skin. This is where hygiene genuinely does matter
```

Two consequences are worth stating explicitly.

**The damage often starts deep.** Load concentrates at the interface between soft tissue and bone,
so the deepest tissue can be injured while the skin surface still looks intact. This is why an
area of intact, discoloured skin — deep purple or maroon — is treated as a serious finding rather
than a bruise, and why such an area can deteriorate quickly once it becomes visible. *The staging
system in use locally will name this category; the categories and their numbering are set by that
system, so the reader's own classification document is the authority for the words.*

**Anatomy predicts the sites.** Where there is little soft tissue between bone and surface, and
where perfusion is poorest, damage comes first — the heels and the sacrum in bed, the ischial
tuberosities in a chair, and the many sites under devices: oxygen tubing behind the ears, mask
edges, casts, splints, tube fixings, compression. *Device-related pressure damage is consensus as
a category and is the one most often missed, because the device is there for a reason and so
nobody looks under it.*

## Why cleanliness is the wrong frame

Because the injury is ischaemic. A scrupulously clean, immobile patient develops pressure damage.
A repositioned one largely does not. Hygiene matters to the microclimate and to infection risk
once skin is broken, and both are real — but they are secondary to load and duration.

There is also a genuine diagnostic distinction here, *and it is consensus*: moisture-associated
skin damage, from incontinence or sweat or exudate, is a different entity from pressure damage,
with a different distribution, different appearance and different management. Confusing the two is
common, and it leads to the wrong intervention in both directions.

Prevention is therefore about load: structured risk assessment with a scored tool *and* clinical
judgement, skin inspection, repositioning, support surfaces, management of moisture, attention to
nutrition and hydration because they alter tissue tolerance and repair, and looking under every
device. *How often to reposition is deliberately not stated here: it is individualised, and the
evidence for any particular interval is genuinely contested in the literature rather than
settled.* The honest answer to "how often" is that it depends on the person, the surface and the
skin response, and that the local policy sets the starting point.

## The human stakes, said plainly

Pressure damage hurts. It is slow, it can be deep, it can take months, it can become the reason
someone cannot go home, and a large share of it is preventable. It is also one of the few harms
that is mostly a property of the care system rather than of the illness — which is why it is
measured, reported and audited the way it is.

That cuts both ways and the second half matters too. Some pressure damage occurs despite
appropriate care, in people whose perfusion or tissue tolerance cannot be fixed, and treating
every instance as negligence is both untrue and corrosive to the reporting that makes prevention
possible.

## What an examiner digs into next

What a particular dressing class is doing to moisture, and what the signs are that the choice was
wrong in each direction. Why the frequency of dressing change is a trade-off rather than a virtue.
The difference between pressure damage and moisture-associated skin damage. Why a discoloured but
intact area over a bony prominence is urgent. Which devices on a given patient need skin inspected
under them. And what the local risk-assessment tool scores, and what it does not.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

* The reader's institutional wound-care formulary and dressing-selection guide — the authority for
  which product is used for which wound locally.
* The international pressure-injury prevention and treatment guideline used in the reader's
  country, and the classification system it carries, for staging language and for prevention
  components.
* The reader's institutional pressure-ulcer prevention policy and its risk-assessment tool, for
  what is scored and what the repositioning starting point is.
* The reader's national guidance on pressure-ulcer prevention and on wound management, for the
  points marked as consensus above.
* A standard tissue-viability or wound-care textbook, for moist wound healing, the dressing
  classes and the TIME framework.
* The published research on repositioning frequency and on support surfaces, for the claim that
  the optimal interval is contested — this is the claim in this answer most worth reading the
  primary literature on.
* Guidance on moisture-associated skin damage from the reader's national tissue-viability body,
  for the distinction from pressure damage.

## Scope and safety

This explains two mechanisms, for someone already training in or qualified for clinical practice.
It is not a protocol, not a decision aid, and it names no product, no dressing brand and no
repositioning interval, deliberately. Dressing selection, risk assessment, staging language and
repositioning frequency are all set by local policy and the local formulary, which are the
authority; this is not, and it has had no clinical review. Nothing here is for use in an emergency
or for a decision about any person's care, including a decision about anyone's own wound. If
someone is unwell right now, the local emergency number is the correct response.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The mechanisms are stable: moist wound healing has been the foundation of wound care for decades,
and pressure damage has been understood as load multiplied by time for longer than that. What
dates is everything procedural — staging terminology and its numbering, risk-assessment tools,
support surface classifications, repositioning recommendations, and above all the formulary, which
changes whenever procurement does. The reader's own policy and formulary are the authority for all
of it.
answer_pokemon:
# A Damp Rock does not make rain. It makes the rain last eight turns instead of five.

That sentence is the whole of what a dressing is. **Rain Dance** sets the weather for five turns.
A **Damp Rock** held by the Pokémon that sets it makes the same weather last **eight**. The rock
adds no power, changes no type match-up and heals nobody. Its single function is to **hold a
condition for longer**, and the games have an entire family of items that do nothing else:

```
   the item               what it holds                   what it does NOT do
   ─────────────────────  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────────────────
   Damp Rock              Rain Dance, 5 turns → 8          set the rain, or heal anything
   Heat Rock              Sunny Day, 5 → 8                 make the sun stronger
   Icy Rock               the hail, 5 → 8                  change what hail does
   Smooth Rock            Sandstorm, 5 → 8                 protect its holder from it
   Light Clay             Light Screen and Reflect, 5 → 8  improve either screen
   Terrain Extender       the terrains, 5 → 8              choose which terrain
```

The repair is the Pokémon's own, and the games are explicit about that too. **Regenerator**
restores a third of a Pokémon's maximum HP when it leaves the field. **Shed Skin** gives it a
one-in-three chance, every single turn, of clearing its own status. **Natural Cure** clears the
slot the moment it switches out. None of that is the weather's doing. The weather only decides
whether the Pokémon gets the chance.

## Moisture balance, and why the target is the middle

Both ends of the weather are a cost, and they are different costs — which is exactly why there are
rocks for both.

```
   TOO MUCH SUN                      right                        TOO MUCH RAIN
   ───────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────
   Solar Power raises     │  the condition you chose,  │  Swift Swim doubles the wrong
   Special Attack and     │  held for as long as you   │  Pokémon's Speed
   costs its holder HP    │  needed it and no longer   │  Fire moves weakened to half
   every single turn      │                            │  Thunder and Hurricane now
   Dry Skin takes EXTRA   │                            │  never miss
   damage in harsh sun    │                            │  Dry Skin holders gain HP
   ───────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────
   what you are choosing:  bring moisture IN  ◄──────────►  take moisture OUT

   And there is a field that is simply hostile: Sandstorm takes a sixteenth of maximum
   HP off everything on the field every turn EXCEPT Rock, Ground and Steel types. A
   wound bed left in the wrong environment is in a Sandstorm.
```

So nobody picks the rock first. You decide which condition the Pokémon needs, and then you pick
the item that holds that condition — which is the right order for every dressing decision there
has ever been. And you look at the field before you decide: what tissue is there, whether anything
is inflamed, how wet it is, what the edges are doing.

## The other problem is load multiplied by turns

The binding moves are the sharpest mechanic in the games for this, because they are not about
damage per hit at all.

**Whirlpool**, Wrap, Bind, Fire Spin and Clamp all do the same three things: they take a share of
the target's HP at the end of every turn, they last several turns, and **the target cannot switch
out**. That last clause is the injury. Not the hit — the inability to get away from it.

And the games have an item for each half of the equation:

```
   Grip Claw       pins the hold at SEVEN turns          ◄── the TIME half
   Binding Band    deepens the share taken each turn     ◄── the PRESSURE half

   pressure
     ^
   high │ ■            a Binding Band bind, briefly
        │   ■
        │      ■
        │          ■ ■
        │                 ■  ■  ■            a Grip Claw bind, for seven turns
    low │                          ■  ■  ■  ■
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────►  turns
                                                            held

   Both points are ON the curve. Hard and short, or soft and long, is the same damage.
   "It was only a few turns" is not an argument, and neither is "it was barely pressing".

   Three things make it worse than the arithmetic says:
     SLIDING    being dragged rather than lifted. Layers move against each other
     RUBBING    Rough Skin, Iron Barbs and a Rocky Helmet all hurt whatever makes
                CONTACT, regardless of how hard the hit was. Contact is its own damage
     THE FIELD  a Pokémon already sitting in the wrong weather tolerates less of
                everything else
```

**And the damage can land after the turn it was done.** **Future Sight** is used now and strikes
at the end of the second turn *after* it was used. In between, the field looks completely
untouched — no animation, no message, nothing on the HP bar. **Doom Desire** behaves the same way.
An attack has already been made, the arithmetic is already settled, and the screen will not show
you for two turns. That is the single most important thing to know about load injury: a patch of
skin that is discoloured but unbroken is a Future Sight that has already been used.

**Anatomy decides where it lands first.** **Onix** has a base Defence of **160** and a base HP of
**35**. Enormously hard on the outside, and almost nothing underneath to lose. Anywhere bone sits
close to the surface is an Onix, and that is where the first damage appears — the heels, the
sacrum, and every point under something you attached on purpose.

## Why clearing the field is the wrong idea

**Defog** removes entry hazards, removes **Light Screen** and **Reflect**, lowers the opponent's
evasion, and in the later games clears the terrain as well. It clears the field of effectively
everything you can see on it. It does **not** loosen a bind by a single turn.

That is the whole objection to treating load injury as a hygiene problem. The things you can see
and tidy are not the thing holding the Pokémon in place. What ends a bind is **Rapid Spin**, or
switching out — getting the load off. Nothing else in the game does it, and no amount of clearing
the visible field substitutes.

Which does not mean the field is irrelevant. A Pokémon in a **Sandstorm** is losing a sixteenth a
turn on top of the bind, so the weather genuinely makes the bind worse — it is simply not the
bind.

And the thing attached on purpose is often the thing doing harm. A **Life Orb** costs its holder a
share of maximum HP every time it attacks. **Black Sludge** damages anything that is not a
Poison-type. An **Iron Ball** halves Speed. Every one of those was equipped deliberately, for a
reason, and every one needs looking under.

How many turns you can leave a Pokémon in before it is too long is the one question this answer
will not answer, because it depends on the Pokémon — and in the clinical case the equivalent
interval is genuinely contested rather than settled.

## Where the metaphor stops

The two mechanisms above are mechanisms. What they are attached to is not.

Pressure damage hurts. It is slow, it can be deep, it can take months to close, it can be the
reason someone does not get home, and a large share of it is preventable. It is also one of the
few harms that is mostly a property of the care system rather than of the illness, which is why it
is counted and reported the way it is.

And the other half, which matters too: some of it happens despite entirely appropriate care, in
people whose perfusion or tissue tolerance cannot be fixed by anybody. Treating every instance as
somebody's failure is both untrue and corrosive to the reporting that prevention depends on.

## What Nurse Joy is listening for

Which direction a given item is moving the moisture, and what it looks like when the choice was
wrong in each direction. Why changing a dressing often is a cost and not a virtue. The difference
between damage from load and damage from being wet. Why an intact but discoloured patch over a
bony prominence is urgent rather than reassuring. Which of the things attached to this patient
need looking under. And what the local risk tool scores — and what it misses.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

* The reader's institutional wound-care formulary and dressing-selection guide — the authority for
  which product is used for which wound locally.
* The international pressure-injury prevention and treatment guideline used in the reader's
  country, and the classification system it carries, for staging language and for prevention
  components.
* The reader's institutional pressure-ulcer prevention policy and its risk-assessment tool, for
  what is scored and what the repositioning starting point is.
* The reader's national guidance on pressure-ulcer prevention and on wound management.
* A standard tissue-viability or wound-care textbook, for moist wound healing, the dressing
  classes and the structured wound-assessment framework.
* The published research on repositioning frequency and on support surfaces, for the claim that
  the optimal interval is contested — the claim here most worth reading the primary literature on.
* Guidance on moisture-associated skin damage from the reader's national tissue-viability body,
  for the distinction from load injury.

Separately, and unlike the above: the weather durations, the item effects, the base stats and the
Future Sight timing in this answer were checked against the games' published data and their public
disassemblies, which this environment could reach.

## Scope and safety

This explains two mechanisms, for someone already training in or qualified for clinical practice.
It is not a protocol, not a decision aid, and it names no dressing product and no repositioning
interval, deliberately — the only durations in it are a video game's. Dressing selection, risk
assessment, staging language and repositioning frequency are set by local policy and the local
formulary, which are the authority; this is not, and it has had no clinical review. Nothing here
is for use in an emergency or for a decision about any person's care, including a decision about
anyone's own wound. If someone is unwell right now, the local emergency number is the correct
response.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The mechanisms are stable: keeping a wound in the right moisture range has been the foundation of
wound care for decades, and load injury has been understood as pressure multiplied by time for
longer. What dates is everything procedural — staging terminology, risk-assessment tools, support
surface classifications, repositioning recommendations, and above all the formulary, which changes
whenever procurement does. The reader's own policy is the authority for all of it. The rocks, by
contrast, have held five turns to eight since Sinnoh.

question: What does a fluid balance chart actually measure, what does it miss, and how does it connect to the circulation?
answer_serious:
# The chart is a ledger of measured volumes. The patient is not a ledger.

A fluid balance chart records the volumes somebody measured going in — oral and enteral intake,
intravenous fluids, intravenous drugs and their diluents, line flushes, blood products — and the
volumes somebody measured coming out: urine, vomit or nasogastric aspirate, stoma output, drain
output, measured stool. It subtracts the second from the first and carries a cumulative balance
forward. *What belongs in each column is consensus across major guidance; the design of the chart
and how the cumulative total is presented are local.*

Two things follow immediately and are worth saying before anything else. **The chart is a trend
instrument, and its unit of meaning is days, not shifts.** And **every quantity on it is a
measured volume**, which means the chart's relationship to the patient's actual fluid state is
mediated by everything that was not measured.

```
   ┌──────────── MEASURED, and therefore on the chart ───────────────────────────┐
   │  IN                                   OUT                                   │
   │  oral and enteral intake              urine                                 │
   │  intravenous fluids                   vomit / nasogastric aspirate          │
   │  drugs and their diluents             stoma output                          │
   │  line flushes                         drain output                          │
   │  blood products                       measured stool                        │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                 │                                      ▲
                 │                                      │
   ┌─────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
   │  NOT MEASURED, and therefore invisible to the arithmetic                    │
   │                                                                             │
   │  INSENSIBLE LOSSES — respiratory and transcutaneous water, continuous,      │
   │    and INCREASED by fever, tachypnoea, a warm environment, large open       │
   │    wounds and burns. The sicker the patient, the larger the thing the       │
   │    chart cannot see                                                         │
   │  UNRECORDED INTAKE — sips, a relative's cup of tea, a drink at a            │
   │    bedside nobody charted                                                   │
   │  UNRECORDED OUTPUT — sweat, incontinence, a leaking dressing or drain,      │
   │    diarrhoea that was not measured                                          │
   │  DISTRIBUTION — see below. This is the big one                              │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Distribution: why a balanced chart is not a reassuring chart

The chart counts fluid crossing the boundary of the body. It says nothing whatever about **where
inside the body** that fluid now is, and that is the question clinical decisions actually turn on.

```
   total body water                       the compartment that matters
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
   │                              │       │  INTRAVASCULAR       │
   │   interstitial  ████████████ │       │  ░░░                 │  ◄── perfusion
   │   oedema, ascites, pleural   │       │                      │      comes from
   │   fluid, fluid in the gut    │       │  depleted            │      HERE only
   │                              │       └──────────────────────┘
   │   intravascular  ░░░         │
   └──────────────────────────────┘
          overloaded in total                 and empty where it counts

   A patient can be SIMULTANEOUSLY fluid-overloaded and intravascularly depleted, and
   it is common — capillary leak in sepsis, low plasma oncotic pressure, accumulation
   in a third space. The chart shows a positive cumulative balance. The circulation is
   underfilled. BOTH readings are correct, because they are measuring different things.
```

This is the central reason the chart cannot be used alone: *that overload and intravascular
depletion coexist is consensus and is mechanism rather than guideline*, and no arithmetic on
measured volumes can distinguish the two.

**Weight is the better integrator.** Daily weight, on the same scales, at the same time, in
comparable clothing, captures everything the ledger missed, because mass is conserved and water is
heavy — over days, a change in weight is overwhelmingly a change in water. *This is consensus.*
Its limits are honest ones: different scales disagree, it is impractical for some patients, and
over weeks it starts to include real tissue mass change. Over days it is the strongest single
measurement of fluid state available at a bedside.

## Urine output as a circulation signal

The kidney receives a large share of cardiac output and is highly sensitive to a fall in
perfusion, so **urine output works as an early surrogate for circulatory adequacy** — not as a
measure of it. When perfusion falls, whether because the circulation is underfilled or because the
heart is not delivering, urine output tends to fall before blood pressure does. *This is consensus
across major guidance, and it is why urine output is monitored at all rather than merely
totalled.*

What breaks the inference, and every one of these matters:

```
   observation                        what it might mean instead of hypovolaemia
   ─────────────────────────────────  ──────────────────────────────────────────────
   output is low                      a BLOCKED OR KINKED CATHETER. Mechanically the
                                      commonest explanation on a ward, and the first
                                      thing checked before anything is concluded
                                      about the kidney
   output is low                      intrinsic kidney injury, or obstruction above
                                      the bladder; also normal antidiuresis in a
                                      post-operative patient
   output looks adequate              an osmotic diuresis — high blood glucose, or
                                      contrast — so volume is being lost, not
                                      conserved
   output looks adequate              a diuretic has been given, which decouples
                                      output from perfusion entirely
   output looks adequate              impaired concentrating ability, common with age
                                      and in chronic kidney disease, so a normal
                                      volume carries less information
   output rises sharply               post-obstructive diuresis, which is a finding
                                      to act on rather than a reassurance
```

*Thresholds for oliguria are expressed per kilogram per hour and are set by local guidance;* they
are deliberately not stated here, because the numbers differ between definitions and between
institutions and the principle does not depend on them.

## Where the chart fails as a measurement

**Completion.** *Audits of fluid chart completeness repeatedly find them incomplete,* and the
cumulative total inherits the error of the worst-documented shift. A chart with one blank column
is not a chart with slightly less information; the cumulative balance is simply wrong from that
point forward, and silently.

**Granularity.** Volumes are recorded in round numbers from vessels of approximate capacity. The
chart is accurate to something much coarser than the figure it prints.

**It is read as a verdict rather than a trend.** A single shift's balance is noise. The slope
across days is the measurement.

**It is not in the early warning score.** Fluid state is absent from the standard composite
observation scores, which is a design limitation of those scores and not an indication that it
does not matter. The two instruments are read together.

So the chart belongs inside a composite clinical assessment, alongside heart rate, blood pressure
and pulse pressure, capillary refill time, peripheral temperature, mucous membranes, jugular
venous pressure, consciousness, and the relevant biochemistry. *Skin turgor is unreliable in older
people and this is consensus* — it is one of the first bedside signs taught and one of the least
dependable.

## The human stakes, said plainly

Getting this wrong harms people in both directions, and the second direction is the one that gets
underestimated.

Under-replacement causes hypoperfusion, kidney injury, delirium, falls, and in the frail older
patient a cascade that is hard to reverse. Over-replacement causes pulmonary oedema,
breathlessness, prolonged ventilation, poor wound healing and an oedematous patient who cannot
mobilise. A fluid chart is a tedious piece of paperwork that is, in practice, one of the few
continuously collected measurements of whether a patient's circulation is being managed correctly,
and it is among the most commonly incomplete documents on a ward. Both of those facts are true at
once and the second is the reason the first is worth insisting on.

## What an examiner digs into next

Why insensible losses rise in exactly the patients whose charts matter most. How a positive
cumulative balance and intravascular depletion coexist, and what else to examine to tell them
apart. Why daily weight outperforms the chart, and what weakens it. The confounder list for urine
output, starting with the catheter. What the local definition of oliguria is and what it is
expressed per. And why fluid state is not in the early warning score, and what is done about that.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

* The fluid balance chart and fluid management policy in use in the reader's own institution — the
  authority for what is charted, how the cumulative total is presented, and what the local
  oliguria definition and escalation point are.
* The reader's national guidance on intravenous fluid therapy in hospital, for assessment,
  monitoring and the reasoning behind replacement decisions.
* The reader's national or international guidance on acute kidney injury, for urine output as a
  monitoring parameter and for its confounders.
* A standard renal or applied physiology textbook, for the compartment reasoning and for
  insensible losses, which are mechanism rather than guideline.
* The reader's institutional audit of fluid chart completion, if one exists, for the
  measurement-quality claim — this is the claim here a reviewer should check first, because its
  strength depends entirely on which audit is read.
* Guidance on hydration and fluid management in older people and in frailty from the reader's
  national body, for the concentrating-ability and skin-turgor points.

## Scope and safety

This explains what a measurement is and is not, for someone already training in or qualified for
clinical practice. It is not a protocol, not a decision aid, and it contains no volumes, no
replacement regimens and no thresholds, deliberately. Fluid prescribing, oliguria definitions and
escalation points are set by local guidance, which is the authority; this is not, and it has had
no clinical review. Nothing here is for use in an emergency or for a decision about any person's
care, including any decision about how much anyone should drink. If someone is unwell right now,
the local emergency number is the correct response.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The physiology does not move: compartments, insensible losses, the kidney's sensitivity to
perfusion, and the conservation of mass that makes weight the better integrator. What dates is the
guidance wrapped around it — fluid therapy recommendations, the choice and composition of
replacement fluids, acute kidney injury definitions and their urine output criteria, and the chart
design itself, which is increasingly electronic and in some places automatically totalled. The
reader's own policy and chart are the authority for every number.

```

                 │                                      ▲
                 │                                      │
   ┌─────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
   │  NOT COUNTED, and therefore invisible to the arithmetic                     │
   │                                                                             │
   │  THE WEATHER — a Sandstorm takes a sixteenth off everything that is not     │

   │    Pokémon is in, the bigger the thing the ledger cannot see                │
   │  WHAT SOMEONE ELSE DID — a berry eaten automatically off the field, a       │
   │    Pokémon healed while you were not looking                                │
   │  WHERE IT WENT — see below. This is the big one                             │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Two things follow before anything else. **The ledger is a trend instrument**, and one turn's entry
is noise. And **every entry is something somebody counted**, so the ledger's relationship to the
Pokémon's actual state runs entirely through what nobody counted.

Which is why the HP bar exists. The exact number on the summary screen is not an estimate and it
does not inherit a missed turn — it is the net, after everything, including the Sandstorm you
forgot. The arithmetic is only as good as the worst-recorded turn. The number is just right.

## Where it went: why a balanced ledger is not a reassuring ledger

**Substitute** costs a quarter of the user's maximum HP and builds a decoy that holds exactly that
much. The HP came off the bar. It did not leave the battle.

```
   everything the Pokémon has             the part that actually takes hits
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
   │                              │       │  the Pokémon itself  │
   │  the Substitute ████████████ │       │  ░░░                 │  ◄── everything
   │  a quarter of maximum HP,    │       │                      │      that matters
   │  standing in front, taking   │       │  nearly empty        │      happens HERE
   │  the hits, holding HP that   │       └──────────────────────┘
   │  can never come back         │
   │                              │
   │  the Pokémon ░░░             │
   └──────────────────────────────┘
          plenty of HP in the room             and almost none where it counts
```

That is the whole point. A Pokémon behind a fat **Substitute** with a nearly empty bar has HP
accounted for and HP unavailable at the same time, and no sum over the ledger can tell the two
apart. **Belly Drum** is the same lesson in one action rather than many: it halves the user's
maximum HP outright to drive Attack to +6, the biggest single swing in the game, and nothing in a
per-turn ledger predicted it.

## The resource that runs out first

Here is the part people miss. **PP, not HP, is usually what runs out.**

PP is counted in four small separate columns, one per move, and the games enforce the **Four-Move
Limit** so there are never more than four. When all four reach zero the Pokémon is reduced to
**Struggle** — it attacks anyway, with nothing, and hurts itself doing it. A full HP bar and four
empty columns is a Pokémon that cannot do the thing you are relying on it for, and the bar will
tell you nothing about it at all.

So the small columns are an early warning that the big number does not carry. And like every early
warning they can be read wrong:

```
   what you see                       what it might mean instead
   ─────────────────────────────────  ──────────────────────────────────────────────
   the move cannot be used            DISABLE. The PP is there. The move is simply
                                      blocked from outside, and nothing about the
                                      Pokémon has changed. CHECK THIS FIRST before
                                      concluding anything about the Pokémon
   the move cannot be used            Taunt, if it is a status move; Encore, if it is
                                      being forced to repeat a different one
   PP is gone and nothing was used    somebody took it. Spite removes PP from the
                                      last move used without it being spent
   PP looks fine                      a Leppa Berry restored 10 of it automatically.
                                      The reading was repaired; the problem that
                                      emptied it was not
   PP looks fine                      an Ether put 10 back into one move, or a
                                      Max Elixir refilled all four — so the reading
                                      is now about the bag, not the Pokémon
```

The Disable line is the one to hold onto. It is the only entry in the table where the correct
first action is to check the equipment rather than examine the Pokémon, and it is also the
commonest.

## Where the ledger fails as a measurement

**A missing turn is not a small error.** Leave one turn out and the cumulative total is wrong from
there on, permanently and silently. It does not degrade — it breaks.

**It is coarser than it looks.** A sixteenth of maximum HP on a Pokémon with 9 HP is rounded to 1,
because the game refuses to let it be zero. Every figure in the column is a rounding of something.

**One turn is not a reading.** The slope across many turns is the measurement.

**And it is not on the main screen.** None of this appears in the status slot or the stat stages —
the composite read from the summary screen and this ledger are two instruments, read together, and
neither contains the other.

## Where the metaphor stops

The mechanism above is a mechanism. What it is attached to is not, and it goes wrong in both
directions.

Too little fluid causes poor perfusion, kidney injury, delirium, falls, and in a frail older
person a cascade that is hard to reverse. Too much causes fluid on the lungs, breathlessness,
longer time on a ventilator, wounds that will not heal, and a swollen patient who cannot get out
of bed. The second direction is the one that gets underestimated, and it is iatrogenic — it is
something done to a patient rather than something that happened to them.

A fluid balance chart is one of the dullest documents on a ward and one of the few continuous
measurements of whether a person's circulation is being managed correctly. It is also among the
most frequently left incomplete. Both of those are true at once, and the second is the reason the
first is worth insisting on at the end of a long shift.

## What Nurse Joy is listening for

Why the thing the ledger cannot see gets *bigger* in exactly the Pokémon whose ledger matters
most. How a healthy-looking total and an empty bar sit together, and what else to look at to tell
them apart. Why the exact number beats the sum of the increments. The whole confounder list for
the small columns, starting with **Disable**. And why none of this appears on the status screen,
and what is done about that.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

* The fluid balance chart and fluid management policy in use in the reader's own institution — the
  authority for what is charted, how the cumulative total is presented, and what the local
  oliguria definition and escalation point are.
* The reader's national guidance on intravenous fluid therapy in hospital, for assessment,
  monitoring and the reasoning behind replacement decisions.
* The reader's national or international guidance on acute kidney injury, for urine output as a
  monitoring parameter and for its confounders.
* A standard renal or applied physiology textbook, for the compartment reasoning and for the
  continuous unmeasured losses, which are mechanism rather than guideline.
* The reader's institutional audit of fluid chart completion, if one exists, for the
  measurement-quality claim — the claim here a reviewer should check first, because its strength
  depends entirely on which audit is read.
* Guidance on hydration and fluid management in older people and in frailty from the reader's
  national body.

Separately, and unlike the above: the fractions, the restored amounts, the Four-Move Limit and the
item and move effects in this answer were checked against the games' published data and their
public disassemblies, which this environment could reach.

## Scope and safety

This explains what a measurement is and is not, for someone already training in or qualified for
clinical practice. It is not a protocol, not a decision aid, and it contains no clinical volumes,
no replacement regimens and no thresholds, deliberately — every number in it belongs to a video
game. Fluid prescribing, oliguria definitions and escalation points are set by local guidance,
which is the authority; this is not, and it has had no clinical review. Nothing here is for use in
an emergency or for a decision about any person's care, including any decision about how much
anyone should drink. If someone is unwell right now, the local emergency number is the correct
response.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The physiology does not move: compartments, continuous unmeasured losses, the kidney's sensitivity
to perfusion, and the conservation of mass that makes a weight better than a sum. What dates is
the guidance wrapped around it — fluid therapy recommendations, replacement fluid composition,
acute kidney injury definitions and their urine output criteria, and the chart itself, which is
increasingly electronic and sometimes totalled automatically. The reader's own policy is the
authority for every clinical number. Leftovers, by contrast, has restored a sixteenth a turn since
Johto.

question: Why does an identical finding mean something different in general practice than in a hospital clinic, and how does prevalence change what it is worth?
answer_serious:
# The finding does not change. The room does.

Sensitivity and specificity are properties of a test. Predictive value is a property of a test
*and* the population it is used in. A general practice and the clinic it refers into run the same
tests on the same bodies and get systematically different meanings out of them, because the
referral process has already sorted the population before the clinic sees it. The clinic's
patients are the ones somebody else already thought were worth a second look. That is not a detail
about paperwork; it is the single largest term in the arithmetic, and it is why a finding that
justifies action in a clinic can be a near-certain false alarm in a waiting room full of people
who mostly do not have anything *[mechanism, not guideline]*.

The named version of this is Bayes' theorem. The useful version is the two-by-two table, worked
twice.

## The arithmetic, worked

```
   ILLUSTRATIVE NUMBERS ONLY. A hypothetical test with sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%,
   applied to 10 000 people in two different rooms. These are round numbers chosen to make
   the mechanism visible. They are NOT the operating characteristics of any real test, and
   no real test should be assumed to behave like this one.

                      PRIMARY CARE                            REFERRED CLINIC
                  prevalence 1 in 100                      prevalence 30 in 100
   ┌───────────┬────────────┬────────────┐      ┌───────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
   │           │  disease + │  disease − │      │           │  disease + │  disease − │
   ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤      ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
   │  test +   │        90  │       990  │      │  test +   │     2 700  │       700  │
   │  test −   │        10  │     8 910  │      │  test −   │       300  │     6 300  │
   ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤      ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
   │  total    │       100  │     9 900  │      │  total    │     3 000  │     7 000  │
   └───────────┴────────────┴────────────┘      └───────────┴────────────┴────────────┘

   PPV =    90 / (  90 +  990) =   8.3 %        PPV = 2 700 / (2 700 + 700) =  79.4 %
   NPV = 8 910 / (8 910 +  10) =  99.9 %        NPV = 6 300 / (6 300 + 300) =  95.5 %

   Identical test. Identical positive result. Nearly ten times the chance of meaning
   something — and, going the other way, a negative result that was nearly conclusive in
   primary care has become a one-in-twenty miss in the clinic.
```

The same calculation in odds form shows what travels between the two rooms and what does not. The
positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity) = 0.9 / 0.1 = **9**, and it is the
same 9 in both columns. Multiply it by the pre-test odds:

```
   primary care    pre-test odds  1 : 99   ×9 →   9 : 99  =  1 : 11   →   8.3 %
   referred clinic pre-test odds  3 :  7   ×9 →  27 :  7            →  79.4 %

   The likelihood ratio is portable. The prior is local. Learning a test's LR is durable
   knowledge; learning its PPV is knowledge about one population at one moment.
```

## Why the primary-care population is genuinely different

Four mechanisms, none of them about the clinician's skill *[mechanism, not guideline]*:

1. **Low prior probability of serious disease.** Most undifferentiated symptoms in an unselected
   population are self-limiting, and the absolute number of serious diagnoses is small, so the
   false positives of any test outnumber its true positives.
2. **Earlier and less differentiated presentation.** Symptoms arrive before the syndrome has
   assembled itself. A finding that is part of a recognisable pattern downstream arrives alone.
3. **The referral filter.** Referral is a selection mechanism, not a transfer. It enriches the
   downstream population for the thing being looked for, which is exactly why the downstream
   clinic's experience of a finding is a bad guide to the upstream clinic's.
4. **Different question.** Primary care is usually asked to exclude; the clinic is usually asked
   to characterise. Those need different test properties, and a test chosen for one is often the
   wrong instrument for the other.

## What follows for the consultation

* **Ruling out and ruling in are not the same operation.** With a low prior, a highly specific
  test that is positive is informative and a negative one tells you almost nothing you did not
  already believe. With a high prior, that inverts.
* **Time is an instrument.** Re-examining the same person three days later samples a different —
  and usually much more informative — distribution than any single test did, because the
  conditions that matter change over hours to days and the ones that do not, do not. This is the
  most powerful diagnostic tool in primary care and it does not appear on any request form.
* **Spectrum bias is real.** Sensitivity and specificity are not actually constant across
  settings: a test validated on clinic patients with advanced disease will usually perform worse
  on the earlier, milder spectrum seen upstream, so the two-by-two above is optimistic in the
  left-hand column rather than pessimistic.
* **Incidence and prevalence answer different questions.** For an acute presentation the relevant
  prior is how often this presents, not how many people have it.
* **Thresholds are local.** Who gets referred, on what finding, and how fast differs substantially
  between health systems — and that means the prevalence in the downstream clinic, and therefore
  the meaning of the identical finding, differs too *[country-dependent]*.

## The human stakes, said plainly

A low prior probability is a statement about a population, and it is delivered to one person. Both
halves of that sentence are true at once, and the harm lives in the gap between them. Of the
people told that something is probably nothing, a small number have the thing — and for them the
reasoning was not careless, it was correct and it was wrong about them. Holding both of those at
the same time is what makes a significant-event review useful rather than an exercise in blame,
and it is also what makes the safety-net in the next question a requirement rather than a nicety.

The harm runs in the other direction too, and is less often counted. Reading a positive result at
a clinic's predictive value when it was produced in a waiting room sends well people into
investigation they did not need: procedures with their own complications, time away from work and
family, and a lasting change in how someone understands their own body. A cascade of investigation
started by one over-read result is a real injury, and the person at the end of it has no way to
know it was avoidable.

And the part that is not statistical at all. The prior a clinician actually uses is not a
published figure; it is partly an impression of the person in front of them. Where that impression
tracks who someone is rather than what they have — their weight, their first language, a
psychiatric diagnosis in their record, their race, how many times they have been in — then
base-rate reasoning stops being arithmetic and becomes a mechanism for not believing people. This
is a documented pattern, not a theoretical risk, and better arithmetic does not fix it. The
question that does some work is whether the same finding in a different person would have been
given the same weight.

## What an examiner digs into next

Whether the candidate reaches for the likelihood ratio rather than the PPV, and can say why. Then
the asymmetry: which direction the test is being used in, and whether the chosen test is good at
that direction. Then the honest part — that the prior in a given practice population is not a
published number, is estimated from experience, and is the term with the largest uncertainty in
the whole calculation.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

* Any standard clinical-epidemiology or evidence-based-medicine textbook, for the two-by-two
  table, likelihood ratios and the derivation of predictive value from prevalence.
* The published methodology of the diagnostic accuracy study behind any specific test being
  considered — specifically its stated setting and recruitment, which is what determines whether
  its quoted sensitivity and specificity transfer to a primary-care population.
* The suspected-cancer or urgent-referral criteria issued by the national or regional body that
  governs the reader's own practice, for the referral thresholds that set the downstream clinic's
  prevalence *[country-dependent]*.
* Any reporting-standards statement for diagnostic accuracy studies, issued by the relevant
  methodology group, for what a study must disclose about its setting and spectrum.

## Scope and safety

This is revision material about reasoning, written for someone already training in or qualified
for the field. It is not a clinical reference, not a decision aid, and not for use in making a
decision about any person's care. Every number in the worked example is a hypothetical round
figure chosen to make the arithmetic legible; none of them is the measured performance of a real
test, and none should be carried into practice. Referral criteria and the resulting case mix
differ by country, region and institution — local guidance is the authority here, and this is not.
If someone is unwell right now, the relevant action is to contact local urgent care or the local
emergency number, not to read this.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The mechanism described here — that predictive value depends on prevalence while likelihood ratios
do not — is settled and is not expected to move. What does move, and quickly, is which tests are
available in primary care, what their measured operating characteristics are, and the referral
thresholds that set downstream prevalence. All three should be re-checked against current local
guidance rather than taken from here, as of October 2026.

# The rustle is the same rustle. The floor is not the same floor.

Every patch of tall grass in Kanto carries an **encounter table**: ten slots, each holding one
species at one level, and ten fixed slot chances that never vary from table to table — 51, 51, 39,
25, 25, 25, 13, 13, 11 and 3 out of 256. The slot chances are a property of the engine. *What is
in the slots* is a property of the place. So the grass shaking is an identical event everywhere in
the region, and it means something completely different on **Route 1** than it does on the first
floor of **Mt. Moon**, and different again two floors down.

That gap is the whole subject. On Route 1 the table is exactly half **Pidgey** and half
**Rattata** — Pidgey holds slots 1, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10 for 128/256, Rattata holds 2, 3, 4 and 8 for
the other 128 — and no amount of walking will produce a **Clefairy**, because Route 1 has no
Clefairy slot at all. On Mt. Moon 1F the table is 202/256 Zubat, 38/256 **Geodude**, 13/256
**Paras** and 3/256 Clefairy. Identical rustle. Utterly different differential.

## The arithmetic, worked

The reading taken off the battle screen is the level. Hold one finding fixed — *the number reads 8
or higher* — and run it on two floors of the same cave, hunting Clefairy for its **Moon Stone**.

```
   EVERY NUMBER BELOW IS REAL, READ OUT OF THE ENCOUNTER TABLES. The slot chances are
   51 51 39 25 25 25 13 13 11 3 out of 256, in slot order, on every land table in the game.

                  MT. MOON 1F                              MT. MOON B1F
          Clefairy in 1 slot: 3/256 = 1.17%        Clefairy in 1 slot: 11/256 = 4.30%
          (Clefairy there is level 8)              (Clefairy there is level 9)
   ┌───────────┬────────────┬────────────┐  ┌───────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
   │  /256     │  Clefairy  │  not it    │  │  /256     │  Clefairy  │  not it    │
   ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤  ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
   │  lvl ≥ 8  │         3  │       177  │  │  lvl ≥ 8  │        11  │       155  │
   │  lvl < 8  │         0  │        76  │  │  lvl < 8  │         0  │        90  │
   ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤  ├───────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
   │  total    │         3  │       253  │  │  total    │        11  │       245  │
   └───────────┴────────────┴────────────┘  └───────────┴────────────┴────────────┘

   catches everything   3 / 3  = 100 %         catches everything  11 / 11 = 100 %
   clears the rest     76 /253 =  30.0 %       clears the rest     90 /245 =  36.7 %
   worth of a hit       3 /180 =   1.67 %      worth of a hit      11 /166 =   6.63 %

   The same reading. Almost the same screening power. Four times the chance of being
   the Clefairy — because the floor underneath it holds four times as many Clefairy.
```

Run it in odds and the portable part separates from the local part. The ratio of hit rates is 1.00
÷ (1 − 0.300) = **1.43** on 1F and 1.00 ÷ (1 − 0.367) = **1.58** on B1F — practically the same
number, because it is a property of the reading, not of the cave:

```
   Mt. Moon 1F    starting odds   3 : 253   ×1.43 →  0.0170  →   1.67 %
   Mt. Moon B1F   starting odds  11 : 245   ×1.58 →  0.0710  →   6.63 %

   The ratio travels between floors. The starting odds do not. Learning what a reading is
   worth as a ratio is knowledge you keep; learning that level 8 means 1.67 % is knowledge
   about one floor of one cave.
```

Go one floor deeper and the gradient continues: on **Mt. Moon B2F** Clefairy holds two slots,
13/256 and 3/256, for 16/256 = **6.25%**. One cave, three floors, and the identical rustle is
worth 1.17%, then 4.30%, then 6.25%.

## Why the first patch of grass is genuinely a different place

Four mechanisms, none of them about how good the Trainer is:

1. **The thing being hunted is rare where most walking happens.** On Mt. Moon 1F, Zubat holds six
   of the ten slots. Sixty-seven Zubat come out for every Clefairy, so anything that pulls in
   false alarms will pull in far more Zubat than Clefairy however good the reading is.
2. **Everything arrives early and underdeveloped.** Route 1's Pidgey are level 2 to 5. Nothing has
   evolved, nothing has the moves it will eventually have, and the sprite that walks into the
   battle is the least distinguishable version of itself it will ever be.
3. **A filter upstream changes the table downstream — a Repel is exactly that.** The engine rolls
   the slot *first* and only then cancels the encounter if the level is below the lead's. With a
   level-10 lead on B2F, 129/256 of rolls survive and 16 of them are Clefairy: 16/129 = **12.4%**,
   double the unfiltered 6.25%, and no slot in the table was touched. What also happens is that
   the per-step chance of meeting anything at all drops from 10/256 × 256/256 = 3.9% to 10/256 ×
   129/256 = 2.0%. Fewer encounters, each one worth more. That is a referral.
4. **The two jobs are different.** A walk down Route 1 is about establishing that nothing unusual
   is there. Standing in front of a filtered table is about identifying which unusual thing it is.
   A reading chosen for one job is often the wrong instrument for the other.

## What follows at the edge of the grass

* **Confirming and excluding are different operations.** On Route 1, a reading that says "this is
  the rare one" is informative, because almost nothing is; a reading that says "this is the common
  one" told you what you already knew. Deep in the cave that inverts.
* **Steps are an instrument.** The encounter rate is 25/256 per eligible step on Route 1 but only
  10/256 anywhere in Mt. Moon and 8/256 in **Viridian Forest**, where **Pikachu** sits in the last
  two slots at 14/256. A second lap of the same patch samples the table again, and it is the
  cheapest instrument there is — it costs no **Poké Ball** and no **Great Ball**.
* **A reading measured in one place misleads in another.** The level ranges differ by floor, so
  the same reading has 30.0% clearing power on 1F and 36.7% on B1F. It was never one fixed
  property.
* **Rate and table answer different questions.** The **Safari Zone**'s centre area runs at 30/256
  per step — the highest in Kanto, matched only by its own other three areas — and its last slot
  is **Chansey** at 3/256. A high rate is not a high yield.
* **Which table a place has is a local fact.** The same place is not the same place between
  versions: Red's Route 4 holds **Ekans** in four slots where Blue's holds **Sandshrew**, Red's
  Viridian Forest fills six of its eight ordinary slots with Weedle and Kakuna where Blue's fills
  them with Caterpie and Metapod, and slot 9 of the Safari Zone's centre area is **Scyther** in
  Red and **Pinsir** in Blue. Nobody should carry a table across the boundary.

## Where the metaphor stops

A low prior probability is a statement about a population, and it is delivered to one person. Both

people told that something is probably nothing, a small number have the thing — and for them the

and it is also what makes the safety-net in the next question a requirement rather than a nicety.

The harm runs in the other direction too, and is less often counted. Reading a positive result at
a clinic's predictive value when it was produced in a waiting room sends well people into
investigation they did not need: procedures with their own complications, time away from work and
family, and a lasting change in how someone understands their own body. A cascade of investigation
started by one over-read result is a real injury, and the person at the end of it has no way to
know it was avoidable.

And the part that is not statistical at all. The prior a clinician actually uses is not a
published figure; it is partly an impression of the person in front of them. Where that impression

is a documented pattern, not a theoretical risk, and better arithmetic does not fix it. The
question that does some work is whether the same finding in a different person would have been
given the same weight.

## What a Gym Leader is listening for

Whether the Trainer reaches for the ratio rather than the raw percentage, and can say why one
travels and the other does not. Then the direction: is the reading being used to confirm or to
exclude, and is it any good at that direction. Then the honest part — the slot chances are printed
in the engine, but which table a given patch of grass has is something a Trainer learns by walking
it, and that is the term carrying the most uncertainty in the entire calculation.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

* Any standard clinical-epidemiology or evidence-based-medicine textbook, for the two-by-two
  table, likelihood ratios and the derivation of predictive value from prevalence.
* The published methodology of the diagnostic accuracy study behind any specific test being
  considered — specifically its stated setting and recruitment, which is what determines whether
  its quoted figures transfer to a primary-care population.
* The suspected-cancer or urgent-referral criteria issued by the national or regional body that
  governs the reader's own practice, for the thresholds that set a downstream clinic's prevalence
  *[country-dependent]*.
* Any reporting-standards statement for diagnostic accuracy studies, issued by the relevant
  methodology group, for what a study must disclose about its setting and spectrum.

The Pokémon figures are a separate matter and are not covered by the line above. The slot chances,
the per-step encounter rates, the encounter tables for Route 1, Mt. Moon 1F, B1F and B2F, Viridian
Forest, Route 4 and the Safari Zone's centre area, and the order in which the engine rolls a slot
and then applies a Repel, were all read directly from the pret decompilation projects, which this
environment can reach.

This is revision material about reasoning, written for someone already training in or qualified

question: What is safety-netting actually for, and what separates a safety-net that works from reassurance that only sounds like one?
answer_serious:
# Safety-netting is what is done instead of certainty, not after it

A consultation in an unselected population usually ends without a diagnosis, and that is the
normal case rather than a failure. Most presentations are self-limiting, most serious disease is
rare, and most tests available at the point of first contact are not powerful enough to drive the
residual probability of something serious to zero. Safety-netting is the clinical response to that
irreducible residue: a plan that converts an un-excludable diagnosis into a bounded, time-limited,
explicitly triggered one. It is a management decision with a mechanism, not an administrative
flourish at the end *[mechanism, not guideline]*.

The corollary is the part candidates miss. If safety-netting is a substitute for certainty, then
its quality should be judged by whether it would actually catch the case — not by whether
something reassuring was said.

## Red flags: what they are and what they are not

A red flag is a feature whose likelihood ratio is large enough to move a probability across an
action threshold on its own. That definition has two consequences that matter more than any list:

* **Red flags are tuned for specificity, and they therefore have poor sensitivity.** Most serious
  disease, most of the time, presents without them — especially early, which is when it is seen
  first *[consensus]*. A red-flag screen is a rule-in instrument being asked to do a rule-out job.
* **A red-flag list is a threshold, and thresholds are set locally.** Which features trigger an
  urgent referral, at what age, and on what timescale differ substantially between health systems
  and are revised regularly *[country-dependent]*.

Here is what a negative red-flag screen actually leaves behind.

```
   ILLUSTRATIVE NUMBERS ONLY — round figures chosen to show the mechanism. These are not
   the measured properties of any real red-flag rule, and no real rule should be assumed
   to behave like this one.

   10 000 presentations of one symptom, 20 of them serious  (prevalence 1 in 500)
   a red-flag screen that picks up half of the serious cases and 5% of the rest

   ┌───────────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┐
   │                   │  serious      │  not serious  │  total        │
   ├───────────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┤
   │  red flag present │           10  │          499  │          509  │
   │  red flag absent  │           10  │        9 481  │        9 491  │
   ├───────────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┤
   │  total            │           20  │        9 980  │       10 000  │
   └───────────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┘

   before the screen   20 / 10 000 = 1 in  500  = 0.200 %
   after it is negative 10 / 9 491 = 1 in  949  = 0.105 %

   The screen roughly halved the probability. It did not remove it. Ten of the twenty
   serious cases are sitting inside the red-flag-negative group, and the net has to be
   cast over about 950 people to be over each one of them.
```

That last line is the design constraint. A safety-net is applied to a large, mostly well
population, so it has to be cheap, specific and not frightening — and it still has to work.

## The anatomy of a net that works

```
   ┌────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
   │ component          │ a net                            │ reassuring noise           │
   ├────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
   │ what is being       │ the specific diagnosis not yet  │ nothing named              │
   │ watched for        │ excluded, named                  │                            │
   │ trigger            │ an observable change the person  │ "if you feel worse"        │
   │                    │ can actually recognise           │                            │
   │ timeframe          │ a date or an interval            │ open-ended                 │
   │ action             │ a named route, with the out-of-  │ "come back"                │
   │                    │ hours route named too            │                            │
   │ who holds it       │ a scheduled review or an active  │ the person's memory        │
   │                    │ recall, not the person's memory  │                            │
   │ recorded           │ in the notes, so the next        │ in one clinician's head    │
   │                    │ clinician inherits it            │                            │
   │ checked            │ the route was confirmed to exist │ assumed                    │
   │                    │ at the hour it may be needed     │                            │
   └────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘
```

Four of those deserve their reasons stated.

**The trigger has to be recognisable by the person holding it.** A trigger phrased in clinical
terms is not a trigger; it is a test of vocabulary. The useful ones describe something observable
that the person has not seen before and would notice.

**The timeframe is the part that converts uncertainty into a decision.** "This does not look
serious today" and "if this has not settled by a stated date, the reasoning changes" are different
statements, and only the second one has a mechanism. An undated net is a deferral, not a plan.

**Documentation is part of the intervention, not the paperwork afterwards.** The next contact is
frequently with someone else, and the only thing that reliably crosses that boundary is the
record. A net that exists only in the memory of the clinician who made it fails precisely in the
scenario it was designed for — someone returning when that clinician is not there.

**Over-netting degrades the signal.** Because the net is cast over roughly 950 people per case, a
net attached to everything is a net attached to nothing: it generates re-attendance, consumes the
capacity needed for the people who do deteriorate, and teaches the population that the instruction
is ritual. Anxiety is a real harm here and is caused by the net itself.

## The human stakes, said plainly

Diagnostic delay is the mechanism behind a large share of serious harm in first-contact care, and
the two named most often are delayed cancer diagnosis and the deterioration of an infection that
looked unremarkable at first presentation *[consensus]*. These are not abstractions and they are
not the clinician's bad luck; they are, in a substantial proportion of cases, a consequence of a
plan that had no trigger, no date and no record. That is also the hopeful part: it is the kind of
failure that a designed process reduces.

A separate point that belongs in the same place. The people for whom a safety-net is most likely
to fail are the ones least able to re-present — language, work, caring responsibilities, cost,
transport, confidence, or a previous experience of not being believed. A net that assumes an
articulate, available, confident person is not a net for them. Active recall, rather than relying
on return, is the part of this that is actually hard and actually matters.

## What an examiner digs into next

Whether the candidate can state what the residual probability was *after* the consultation, and
whether the net was sized for it. Then the specific wording of a trigger, out loud. Then the
out-of-hours route and whether it was checked. Then the awkward one — what happens when the net is
cast and nobody returns, and how a practice distinguishes a resolved illness from a person who
could not get back.

## Sources

**None of the sources below was retrieved.** They were unreachable from the environment this was
written in, so every claim here rests on general professional knowledge and is attributed, not
quoted. Open the document before relying on anything in this answer.

* The suspected-cancer and urgent-referral criteria issued by the national or regional body
  governing the reader's practice, for the red-flag thresholds themselves *[country-dependent]*.
* The curriculum and assessment guidance of the reader's own college or training body for general
  practice, for what safety-netting is formally expected to contain.
* The reader's own organisation's significant-event and serious-incident framework, which is where
  the local evidence about how nets fail actually lives.
* Any systematic review of diagnostic error and diagnostic delay in primary care, in the
  patient-safety literature, for the recurring contributory factors.
* The national patient-safety or healthcare-inspection body's published reports on diagnostic
  delay for the reader's country *[country-dependent]*.

## Scope and safety

This is revision material about how a clinical process is designed, written for someone already
training in or qualified for the field. It is not a clinical reference, not a decision aid, and
not for use in making a decision about any person's care. It contains no red-flag list on purpose:
the lists are local, they are revised, and the authoritative version is the one issued for the
reader's own setting. The worked numbers are hypothetical round figures illustrating a mechanism
and are not the properties of any real rule. If someone is unwell right now, the relevant action
is to contact local urgent care or the local emergency number, not to read this.

## Where this stands, October 2026

The reasoning here — that safety-netting substitutes for certainty and should therefore be
specified like any other intervention — is mainstream and stable. The red-flag thresholds it
refers to are not: they are revised regularly and differ between countries, so none is reproduced
here. Access routes, out-of-hours arrangements and recall mechanisms also change, including
locally and at short notice, so the route named in any net needs confirming at the time rather
than remembered. Correct as a description of consensus in October 2026.
